introduction: On this Sunday, Moses tells the people that God's word is not far away but very near, in their mouths and in their hearts. In the Gospel, a lawyer asks Jesus, Who is my neighbor? and Jesus answers with the parable of the Good Samaritan, ending with the words, Go and do likewise. Paul sings of Christ, the image of the invisible God. Let us become neighbors to all in need.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God's word is very near to us. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be a Good Samaritan to all who are wounded and left by the roadside. Let us pray to the Lord.
For victims of violence and robbery, and for refugees: that they may find people who stop to help them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For doctors, nurses and all who care for the sick and injured: that God may bless their compassion. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who pass by on the other side: that their hearts may be moved with compassion. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may not ask who is our neighbor, but become a neighbor to everyone. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, your Son came down to bind our wounds like the Good Samaritan. Give us hearts moved with compassion, and help us to go and do likewise. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Go and do likewise
reflection.body:
Moses wants the people to understand that God's commandment is not impossible or far away. "It is not in heaven... Neither is it beyond the sea." Instead, "the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it." We do not need to search far for God's will. We know it already.

In the Gospel, a lawyer asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life. Jesus asks him what the law says, and he answers well: love God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself. Jesus says, "Do this, and you will live." But the lawyer wants to set limits, so he asks, "Who is my neighbor?"

Jesus answers with a story. A man is attacked by robbers and left half dead by the road. A priest passes by on the other side. So does a Levite. Then a Samaritan comes, a foreigner whom many Jews of the time despised. "When he saw him, he was moved with compassion." He bandages the man's wounds, puts him on his own animal, takes him to an inn, pays for his care, and promises to return.

Jesus turns the question around. He asks which of the three "seemed to be a neighbor" to the man. The answer is obvious: "He who showed mercy on him." And Jesus says, "Go and do likewise." The question is not who deserves my help, but whose neighbor I will become.

The Church has long seen Christ himself in the Good Samaritan: he comes down to us, wounded by sin, and binds our wounds. Paul's hymn reminds us who he is: "He is the image of the invisible God," through whom all things were made and through whom God reconciled all things, "having made peace through the blood of his cross."

This week, notice who is lying wounded by your road: someone lonely, ill, struggling or rejected. Stop. Be moved with compassion, and do one concrete thing to help.
